newsitem.title: USA: U.S. March trade gap narrows on record exports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. March trade gap narrows on record exports.

text.p: Record overseas sales helped shrink the U.S. trade deficit by a dramatic 19.3 percent to $8.51 billion during March, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday.
Total exports increased 4.1 percent from February to a record $76.48 billion on strong demand for American-made aircraft, capital goods like telecommunications equipment and consumer goods.
Imports grew a more modest 1.2 percent to $84.99 billion, also a record, kept in check by a lower value of imported cars and parts, primarily from Canada.
The resulting deficit was well below Wall Street economists' forecasts for a $10.3 billion March shortfall.
Previously, the department said the February deficit was $10.42 billion but it revised that up to $10.54 billion. The March deficit was the lowest since a $7.97 billion shortfall last November.

There was a sharp improvement in the monthly deficit with China. The bilateral gap between exports and imports from the Asian trade giant narrowed by 22.4 percent during March to $2.59 billion -- lowest since $2.3 billion in April last year -- from $3.34 billion in February.
But the politically sensitive deficit with Japan swelled to $4.61 billion, an 8.3 percent increase from February's $4.26 billion gap.
The persistent monthly trade deficits with Japan appear to be under steady pressure.

In April numbers released on Monday, Tokyo said that its bilateral surplus with the United States more than doubled in April, on a year-over-year basis, largely because of surging exports. Japan's exports have been fuelled by a weaker yen.

The cost of imported crude oil fell for a second consecutive month during March, down 4 percent to $4.38 billion, as the price per barrel eased to $18.72 from $20.49 in February and from $22.03 in January.
The United States typically runs a surplus on its trade with other countries in services like travel and tourism, which partly offsets big merchandise trade deficits.
In March the merchandise deficit fell 11.4 percent from February to $15.06 billion. The surplus on services climbed 1.3 percent to $6.56 billion.
In trade with Mexico, the United States posted a deficit of $1.47 billion in March, a 23.2 percent jump from February's $1.2 billion shortfall.
The United States had a smaller surplus on trade with Western Europe of $320 million in March, compared with $330 million in February.

Foreign sales of civilian aircraft jumped strongly in March to $2.46 billion from $1.72 billion in February. Commerce officials said much of the gain was accounted for by stronger sales to South Korea and to Saudi Arabia.
Imports of autos and parts from all sources fell by $1.22 billion to $11.09 billion in March from $12.31 billion in February while consumer goods imports eased down by $98 million to $15.14 billion.

But the value of imported capital goods -- including items like semiconductors, pulp and paper machinery and materials handling equipment -- was up by $567 million to a record $20.49 billion in March, reflecting the strong pace of U.S. economic expansion.
